name: Underactive and overactive thyroid
headline: Underactive and overactive thyroid compared: symptoms, causes and treatment
summary: An underactive thyroid makes too little hormone and slows the body down; an overactive thyroid makes too much and speeds it up.
keyPoints: An underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) means the gland does not make enough thyroid hormone; an overactive one (hyperthyroidism) means it makes too much.
Symptoms are broadly opposite: tiredness and feeling cold with an underactive thyroid, weight loss and feeling hot with an overactive one.
The main cause of an underactive thyroid in the UK is an autoimmune condition called Hashimoto's disease.
Underactive thyroid is usually treated with levothyroxine tablets; overactive thyroid with medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery.
Treatment for an overactive thyroid can lead to an underactive thyroid, so follow-up blood tests matter.

body.heading: What does the thyroid do?
body.body: The thyroid is a gland in the neck that makes hormones which help control the body's energy use. When it makes too little hormone the body's processes slow down, and when it makes too much they speed up.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of an underactive thyroid?
body.body:
The NHS describes an underactive thyroid as a common condition in which the thyroid does not make enough hormone. Typical symptoms are tiredness, feeling cold, weight gain, constipation, low mood, and dry skin or hair loss.

Symptoms may be mild and can develop slowly, so they are not always easy to notice.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of an overactive thyroid?
body.body:
The NHS says an overactive thyroid, also called hyperthyroidism, means the thyroid makes too much hormone. Symptoms include nervousness or irritability, difficulty sleeping, persistent tiredness, sensitivity to heat, and a fast or irregular heartbeat.

Weight loss despite a normal or increased appetite and a swelling in the neck, called a goitre, can also occur.

body.heading: What causes each condition?
body.body:
In the UK, the main cause of an underactive thyroid is Hashimoto's disease, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the thyroid.

The main cause of an overactive thyroid is Graves' disease, another autoimmune condition. Thyroid nodules and some medicines can also cause it.

body.heading: How are they treated?
body.body:
An underactive thyroid is usually treated with levothyroxine tablets, which replace the missing hormone. The NHS says they are usually needed for life, with regular blood tests to check that the treatment is right.

An overactive thyroid can be treated with antithyroid medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery. Beta blockers can ease symptoms such as palpitations in the meantime.

Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid that then needs lifelong hormone tablets.

body.heading: How is the thyroid tested, and when should someone get help?
body.body:
Thyroid function is checked with blood tests that measure thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and thyroid hormones. The site's pages on thyroid function tests and TSH explain them, and the laboratory report shows the reference range used.

A GP appointment is the route for symptoms that could be thyroid-related. The NHS advises calling 999 if a thyroid storm, a rare and life-threatening flare-up of an overactive thyroid, is suspected.
